title: Outsourcing fees: Delegation cannot justify double recovery
desc: Preserves professional duties across providers while distinguishing service charges, pass-through costs, consent and continuing oversight.

kps.k: Outsourcing changes who performs legal work, not the responsible lawyer’s professional obligations.
kps.d: The New York City and ABA opinions condition outsourcing on competence, supervision, confidentiality, conflicts safeguards, appropriate billing and lawful delegation. Their reasoning applies existing professional duties rather than establishing a separate outsourcing regime. The 2012 ABA Commission proposes clarifications to Model Rule comments and Rule 5.3’s title, expressly neither endorsing nor rejecting outsourcing. These materials primarily supply ethical interpretation, not empirical proof of successful delivery; jurisdiction-specific law controls, and Florida Opinion 07-2 is expressly nonbinding.

qs.q: The ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20 has concluded that, although changes to the text of the Model Rules are not necessary, Comments to certain Rules should be clarified to address this issue so that lawyers can more easily determine their ethical obligations.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

qs.q: The laws, court rules, regula- tions, rules of professional conduct, and opinions promulgated in individual jurisdic- tions are controlling.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 08-451: Lawyer's Obligations When Outsourcing Legal and Nonlegal Support Services · Regulators & courts · 2008

kps.k: Effective delegation requires provider diligence and continuing oversight, not reliance on credentials alone.
kps.d: The opinions recommend background checks, references, interviews, clear assignments, communication and substantive review adapted to the worker’s experience and the task’s risks. Cross-border differences in training, language, time zones and legal remedies increase the work needed to supervise. The 2009 New York City report advises against retention when adequate supervision cannot be maintained. The 2012 Commission distinguishes direct supervision from monitoring outside services: lawyers must remain aware of performance even where direct control is impracticable. Client-selected providers warrant an agreed allocation of monitoring, but tribunal duties can prevent complete delegation to the client.

qs.q: The word “monitoring” makes clear that there is nevertheless a need to remain aware of how nonlawyer services are being performing.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

qs.q: For example, if a client instructs the lawyer to hire a particular electronic discovery vendor, the lawyer cannot cede all monitoring responsibility to the client,
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

kps.k: Confidentiality and conflicts require safeguards across the provider chain; client consent does not cure every risk.
kps.d: The guidance calls for checking intermediaries’ and workers’ adverse engagements, restricting access to necessary information, and using contractual confidentiality duties, security controls and breach remedies. The 2009 report extends protections to subcontractors; Florida guidance addresses data protection through eventual destruction. Foreign confidentiality protections are not necessarily weaker, and confidentiality differs from privilege. Lawyers must assess data-export restrictions, seizure powers and available remedies. Where federal law prohibits disclosure, the 2009 report requires narrowing or abandoning the assignment rather than relying on consent. Its conflict-checking guidance expressly excludes purely administrative providers.

qs.q: The outsourcing New York lawyer should also ordinarily ask both the intermediary and the non-lawyer performing the legal support service whether either is performing, or has performed, services for any parties adverse to the lawyer’s client.
qs.a: New York City Bar Formal Opinion 2006-3: Outsourcing Legal Support Services Overseas · Regulators & courts · 2006

qs.q: In light of such differing    rules and regulations, an attorney should require sufficient and specific assurances (together with    an outline of relevant policies and processes) that the data, once used for the service requested,    will be irretrievably destroyed, and not sold, used, or otherwise be capable of access after the    provision of the contracted-for service.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Disclosure and consent standards vary with the provider’s role, the lawyer’s control and client expectations.
kps.d: New York City Opinion 2006-3 treats consent as circumstance-dependent, emphasizing confidential disclosures, significant participation, client expectations and non-cost billing. The 2009 report recommends disclosure as the norm for substantive legal outsourcing and generally favors written consent, while acknowledging disagreement over tasks such as patent searches. ABA Opinion 08-451 distinguishes closely controlled temporary lawyers from typical, more attenuated outsourcing relationships, requiring informed consent before sharing protected information in the latter. The 2012 Commission leaves detailed consent questions unresolved and notes that routine scanning or copying ordinarily needs no consent. In the 2009 report’s direct corporate-retention scenario, separate client consent is inapplicable, but internal business-unit communication remains advisable.

qs.q: Thus, where the relationship between the firm and the individuals perform- ing the services is attenuated, as in a typical outsourcing relationship, no information protected by Rule 1.6 may be revealed without the client’s informed consent.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 08-451: Lawyer's Obligations When Outsourcing Legal and Nonlegal Support Services · Regulators & courts · 2008

qs.q: Notably, the proposed Comment language does not describe whether a lawyer must obtain consent when disclosing confidential information to nonlawyer service providers outside the firm.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

kps.k: Billing guidance distinguishes reasonable service fees from pass-through costs and rejects double recovery.
kps.d: New York City Opinion 2006-3 treats overseas nonlawyer work as support rather than legal services and defaults to direct cost plus reasonably allocated associated overhead unless the client specifically agrees otherwise. ABA Opinion 08-451 permits a surcharge for contract-lawyer services within a reasonable total fee, without disclosure of the provider’s compensation, but prohibits marking up disbursements. These positions concern different classifications of work and charges, not a single universal markup rule. ABA and Florida guidance also limit additional charges for supervision or work already covered by the client’s fee.

qs.q: Absent a specific agreement with the client to the contrary, the lawyer should charge the client no more than the direct cost associated with outsourcing, plus a reasonable allocation of overhead expenses directly associated with providing that service.
qs.a: New York City Bar Formal Opinion 2006-3: Outsourcing Legal Support Services Overseas · Regulators & courts · 2006

qs.q: 00-420,6 we concluded that a law firm that engaged a contract lawyer could add a surcharge to the cost paid by the billing lawyer provided the total charge represented a reasonable fee for the services provided to the client.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 08-451: Lawyer's Obligations When Outsourcing Legal and Nonlegal Support Services · Regulators & courts · 2008

kps.k: Supervision is not blanket permission to delegate every legal function, including to computers.
kps.d: New York City Opinion 2006-3 declines the broad position that supervision necessarily makes every nonlawyer task permissible. Florida guidance reserves independent legal judgment for lawyers, while the ABA leaves particular unauthorized-practice determinations to applicable jurisdictions. The 2012 Commission extends its proposed nonlawyer-assistance framework to automated services such as cloud computing, not specifically generative AI. Can Robots Be Lawyers? challenges unrestricted automation under lawyer oversight, arguing against delegating courtroom advocacy and settlement or plea negotiations. The same author questions potentially protectionist UPL enforcement and conditionally supports technology that can perform particular tasks as well as humans to expand access to justice.

qs.q: If an activity requires the independent judgment and participation of the lawyer, it        cannot be properly delegated to a nonlawyer employee.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: But surely some tasks, such as in court advocacy and settlement or plea negotiations,  cannot and should not be delegated to a computer.
qs.a: Can Robots Be Lawyers? Computers, Lawyers, and the Practice of Law · Academia · 2017

kps.k: Potential savings and capacity gains remain contested once supervision, quality and employment effects enter the analysis.
kps.d: ABA Opinion 08-451 identifies lower costs and flexible staffing as potential benefits. The 2012 Commission reports provider safeguards and favorable practitioner experience from research and consultation, but supplies no quantified demonstration of net savings or universal compliance; it also reports that domestic outsourcing predominates. In Mintz’s 2007 reporting, Louis Burke questions substitution in complex specialist work, while Robert Simpson predicts broader provider capabilities but acknowledges supervision and management burdens. Forecasts of offshore job migration are not measured losses. Ribstein’s 2010 argument adds a competitive implication: in-house counsel could supervise providers directly, expand capacity and reduce outside-counsel demand. That remains a possibility, not an established outcome.

qs.q: Outsourcing affords lawyers the ability to reduce their costs and often the cost to the client to the extent that the individuals or entities providing the outsourced services can do so at lower rates than the lawyer’s own staff.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 08-451: Lawyer's Obligations When Outsourcing Legal and Nonlegal Support Services · Regulators & courts · 2008

qs.q: 4          The Commission’s conclusions regarding these issues were informed by scholarly articles, studies, and surveys; testimony offered at the Commission’s public hearings; comments received in response to questions that were posed to clients, lawyers, law firms, and providers of outsourced services; and news reports.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

kps.k: A broader ethical critique asks who benefits beyond the immediate client and provider.
kps.d: Outsourcing and the Globalizing Legal Profession shifts attention from client-facing compliance to American outsourcers’ responsibilities toward India’s legal system. The author distinguishes workers’ private income gains from investment in legal institutions, suspects that little revenue supports institutional improvement, and argues that investors have an economic interest in a better-functioning system. The excerpt offers neither a quantified finding nor a specified remedy. This inquiry differs from both the Commission’s conditional affordability-based access-to-justice argument and domestic employment objections; none establishes the distribution of outsourcing’s gains or harms.

qs.q: As we will see, the ethical obligations discussed here are very different and go to the question of what the American legal outsourcers' responsibility is to the Indian legal environment and system upon which they draw.
qs.a: Outsourcing and the Globalizing Legal Profession · Academia · 2007

qs.q: Also, by reducing the cost of legal services, outsourcing can improve access to justice by making legal services more affordable.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

vlens.an: Within this curated academic and research selection, the clearest shared direction is to accept the proposition that outsourcing or automation does not remove the responsible lawyer’s professional obligations, while extending the analysis beyond billing. Ribstein develops the buyer-side implication: in-house counsel could provide comparable supervision directly, increasing legal-department capacity and potentially reducing reliance on outside firms. The automation scholarship adds substantive limits, arguing that oversight is not blanket permission to delegate every function, and conditionally connects competent automation to access to justice. There is material internal variation: scholarship on global legal outsourcing redirects attention from client-facing duties and fee treatment toward American outsourcers’ responsibilities to India’s legal institutions, while one source cannot be assessed because the supplied excerpt is only bibliographic. These sources do not directly establish or challenge the principal rule against double recovery, and their claims about capacity, savings and institutional effects are mainly conditional or predictive rather than measured findings. Overall, they build on the proposition’s responsibility-and-oversight foundation rather than supplying evidence for its specific billing conclusions.

qs.q: Big Law avoids this problem through a rule that enables lawyers to outsource as long as they exercise reasonable supervision over the supplier.52 Corporate clients could exercise comparable supervision through in-house counsel, which already hire outsourcers to assist them in their own work.
qs.a: The Death of Big Law · Academia · 2010

qs.q: As we will see, the ethical obligations discussed here are very different and go to the question of what the American legal outsourcers' responsibility is to the Indian legal environment and system upon which they draw.
qs.a: Outsourcing and the Globalizing Legal Profession · Academia · 2007

vlens.an: The curated market-analysis and press source supports the cluster’s principal proposition by reporting outsourcing as ethically permissible only when the retaining lawyer continues to bear full professional responsibility and complies with supervision, confidentiality, conflicts, consent and billing duties. In particular, Steven J. Mintz’s article presents delegation as an application of established professional rules rather than a transfer of responsibility, and reports a general direct-cost limitation that aligns with the proposition’s rejection of double recovery. Material internal variation concerns outsourcing’s practical merits, not these core ethical conditions: quoted commentators disagree about likely cost savings, quality in complex work, management burdens and future growth. Those statements are forecasts and professional judgments rather than measured evidence of net benefits or employment losses. The hostile appended reader comment is separate from Mintz’s reporting and should not be attributed to the article’s professional voice.

qs.q: lawyer who outsources work “must at every step shoulder complete responsibility for the nonlawyer’s work” (NYCBA opinion), and “under no circumstances may the non-California attorney ‘tail’ wag the California attorney ‘dog’” (SDCBA opinion).
qs.a: Ethics Opinions Allow Foreign Legal Outsourcing · Market & press · 2007

qs.q: lawyer: Supervise the foreign lawyer’s work, preserve client confidences, avoid conflicts of interest, generally bill only for the direct cost of outsourcing, and obtain advance client consent in certain circumstances.
qs.a: Ethics Opinions Allow Foreign Legal Outsourcing · Market & press · 2007

vlens.an: The selected regulators and professional bodies support the proposition that outsourcing changes the delivery arrangement without transferring the lawyer’s professional responsibility or permitting duplicative billing. Their common rationale is that existing duties—competence, supervision or monitoring, confidentiality, conflicts controls, lawful delegation and reasonable fees—continue across provider boundaries. Material variation concerns billing classification and the specificity of guidance: New York City Opinion 2006-3 generally limits overseas nonlawyer support charges to direct cost plus associated overhead absent client agreement; ABA Opinion 08-451 permits a reasonable service-fee surcharge for contract lawyers but prohibits markup when provider costs are passed through as disbursements and rejects recovering supervision costs twice; Florida expressly rejects a separate charge for work already incorporated into the standard fee. The 2012 ABA Commission and Resolution 105C support the continuing-duties framework but largely rely on existing fee rules rather than developing the service-fee/pass-through distinction. The sources also differ on when disclosure and consent are required and on whether direct supervision or monitoring is practicable, but these are implementation differences rather than opposition to the proposition. These conclusions describe only the curated sources supplied, not regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: But at the same time, to avoid aiding the unauthorized practice of law, the lawyer must at every step shoulder complete responsibility for the non-lawyer’s work.
qs.a: New York City Bar Formal Opinion 2006-3: Outsourcing Legal Support Services Overseas · Regulators & courts · 2006

qs.q: improper to charge separately for work that is usually otherwise accomplished by a client’s own attorney and incorporated into the standard fee paid to the attorney, even if that cost is paid to a third party provider.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundations broadly support the proposition that outsourcing changes the provider of work without transferring the responsible lawyer’s professional duties, and that delegation cannot justify duplicative or improperly marked-up charges. The principal ethics authorities ground outsourcing in existing duties of competence, supervision or monitoring, confidentiality, conflicts, client consent and avoidance of unauthorized practice; they provide normative interpretation rather than empirical evidence that outsourcing consistently produces savings or quality. Their billing rules also require an important classification distinction: New York City’s 2006 opinion generally limits overseas nonlawyer support charges to direct cost plus associated overhead absent client agreement, whereas ABA Opinion 08-451 permits a reasonable service-fee surcharge for contract lawyers but prohibits markups when provider costs are passed through as disbursements and limits separate recovery of supervision costs already covered by legal fees. The 2012 ABA Commission reinforces application of existing rules while remaining neutral on whether outsourcing itself should be endorsed. Material variation lies mainly outside this core: Mintz reports unresolved disagreement over quality and net savings; Ribstein builds on the proposition by predicting that supervised outsourcing could expand in-house capacity and reduce reliance on outside firms; and the globalizing-profession source redirects attention toward outsourcers’ responsibilities to India’s legal system. These curated sources therefore support the proposition overall without establishing the prevalence, success or net economic effects of outsourcing.

qs.q: But at the same time, to avoid aiding the unauthorized practice of law, the lawyer must at every step shoulder complete responsibility for the non-lawyer’s work.
qs.a: New York City Bar Formal Opinion 2006-3: Outsourcing Legal Support Services Overseas · Regulators & courts · 2006

qs.q: If the firm decides to pass those costs through to the client as a disburse- ment, however, no markup is permitted.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 08-451: Lawyer's Obligations When Outsourcing Legal and Nonlegal Support Services · Regulators & courts · 2008

elens.an: The substantive source accepts the proposition’s core premise that delegation leaves the lawyer ultimately responsible, then materially extends it to automation: oversight is not blanket permission to computerize every legal function, and courtroom advocacy and settlement or plea negotiations should remain nondelegable. It also adds a conditional access-to-justice rationale for automation where technology can perform particular tasks as well as humans. This is qualified rather than unreserved: the access benefit is posed conditionally, not established empirically, and the source does not address the proposition’s distinctions among service fees, pass-through costs, consent, or double recovery. Internal variation in the curated evidence is evidentiary rather than oppositional: the other record contains only bibliographic material, so its position cannot be determined.

qs.q: But surely some tasks, such as in court advocacy and settlement or plea negotiations,  cannot and should not be delegated to a computer.
qs.a: Can Robots Be Lawyers? Computers, Lawyers, and the Practice of Law · Academia · 2017

qs.q: This argument applies to  technologies as well—if they can, in fact, perform aspects of legal practice as well as humans,  shouldn’t we use them to increase access to justice?
qs.a: Can Robots Be Lawyers? Computers, Lawyers, and the Practice of Law · Academia · 2017

elens.an: The 2025 Florida Bar packet supports the proposition that outsourcing does not displace the responsible lawyer’s existing professional duties and cannot justify double recovery. Its principal reasoning is doctrinal rather than empirical: overseas paralegal assistance is conditionally permissible only where the lawyer addresses lawful delegation, direct supervision, conflicts, confidentiality and billing. It also directly rejects a separate charge when outsourced work is already incorporated into the lawyer’s standard fee. Material internal variation concerns how those duties apply: foreign providers receive heightened scrutiny because distance, differing legal protections and auditability can complicate supervision and data security; consent and disclosure vary with risk, provider participation and client expectations; and tasks requiring independent legal judgment remain nondelegable. The opinion is advisory and nonbinding, leaves particular unauthorized-practice determinations to the lawyer and applicable law, and does not establish that outsourcing has been adopted successfully at scale. Thus, it supports the cluster’s ethical and billing proposition while supplying jurisdiction-specific guidance rather than evidence of market prevalence or outcomes.

qs.q: A lawyer is not prohibited from engaging the services of an overseas provider to provide paralegal assistance as long as the lawyer adequately addresses ethical obligations relating to assisting the unlicensed practice of law, supervision of nonlawyers, conflicts of interest, confidentiality, and billing.
qs.a: Ethics Informational Packet — Technology: Florida Bar Ethics Opinions Related to Technology (including Opinion 24-1 on generative AI and Opinion 25-1) · Regulators & courts · 2025
